chapters.n: Abraham opens his record in Ur, the home of his ancestors in the land of the Chaldeans (southern Mesopotamia). He realizes he must find a new home — the first step in a life of faith-driven journeys.

f.g: A people of southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq); Ur is called “Ur of the Chaldees” in Genesis 11:28, 31.

chapters.n: Abraham describes what he longs for: peace, greater righteousness and knowledge, to be a father of many nations, and the priesthood blessings of the patriarchs. Through seeking and obedience he becomes a rightful heir and High Priest.

f.g: A phrase also used of Melchizedek (Alma 13:18), Abraham’s priesthood leader (D&C 84:14).

chapters.n: This priesthood was passed down from Adam — the first father — through the patriarchs to Abraham. Its roots even reach back before the earth was formed.

f.g: The birthright of patriarchal priesthood leadership, passed from father to son.

chapters.n: Abraham sought to be appointed to the priesthood in the same way God had appointed his forefathers, with special concern for his future “seed,” or descendants.
Abraham’s own family had abandoned God’s commandments to worship heathen idols, and they refused to listen to him. His faith began in a home that did not share it.

f.g: peoples who did not worship the true God.

chapters.n: Abraham names the gods his fathers turned to — Elkenah, Libnah, Mahmackrah, Korash, and the god of Pharaoh. These names are unknown outside this record; some scholars have suggested links to ancient Near Eastern deities.

f.g: Possibly related to the Semitic title ’el qoneh, “God, creator/possessor” (compare Genesis 14:19).

chapters.n: These idol worshippers even sacrificed children, and they tried to kill Abraham through the priest of Elkenah, who also served Pharaoh. “Dumb” idols means mute ones that cannot speak or act.

f.g: dumb = unable to speak; lifeless images.

chapters.n: Abraham explains that it was customary for Pharaoh’s priest to sacrifice men, women, and children on an altar in Chaldea, showing Egyptian religious influence reaching into Mesopotamia.

f.g: foreign gods, not the God of Israel.

chapters.n: The priest offers sacrifices to Pharaoh’s god and to the sun god called Shagreel, following Egyptian ritual.

f.g: Identified in the text as the sun; several ancient cultures worshipped a sun deity.

chapters.n: Even a child was sacrificed as a “thank-offering” on the altar at Potiphar’s Hill, at the edge of the plain of Olishem. Abraham gives specific place names, rooting his story in real geography.

f.g: Some scholars have pointed to an ancient inscription naming a place called Ulisum in northern Mesopotamia.
a sacrifice given in gratitude to a god.

chapters.n: The priest had killed three young women, royal descendants of Ham, because they refused to worship idols of wood and stone. Their virtue cost them their lives — they are among scripture’s early martyrs.

f.w: gods of wood or of stone

chapters.n: The priests seize Abraham to kill him the same way. Abraham refers readers to an illustration at the beginning of his record — Facsimile 1 in the Pearl of Great Price.

f.w: the representation at the commencement of this record
f.g: Facsimile 1, printed at the start of the Book of Abraham.

chapters.n: The altar was shaped like a bed frame and stood before the idols. Facsimile 1 depicts such a lion-shaped couch.

f.g: the frame of a bed.

chapters.n: Abraham says he has drawn the idols in the opening figures, which the Chaldeans called “Rahleenos,” meaning hieroglyphics — picture-writing.

f.g: Given in the text as the Chaldean word for hieroglyphics; not attested elsewhere.
the picture-based writing system of ancient Egypt.

chapters.n: As the priests raise their hands to kill him, Abraham cries to God. The Lord hears, fills him with a vision, and an angel instantly loosens his bonds.
The Lord speaks by name — Jehovah — and promises to deliver Abraham and lead him from his family to a land he does not know. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.w: a strange land which thou knowest not of

chapters.n: Jehovah explains that He has come down to judge these idol worshippers and to destroy the man who tried to kill Abraham — whom He calls “my son.”

f.g: A tender title expressing covenant relationship with God.

chapters.n: The Lord promises to lead Abraham personally, to put His name upon him — the priesthood of his fathers — and to cover him with divine power.

f.w: to put upon thee my name

chapters.n: As with Noah, God will make Abraham the head of a new beginning; through Abraham’s ministry God’s name will be known forever.

f.w: my name shall be known in the earth forever

chapters.n: The Lord destroys the altar and idols and strikes down the priest, causing mourning in Chaldea and Pharaoh’s court. Abraham explains that “Pharaoh” is a title meaning king by royal blood.

f.g: An Egyptian royal title (literally “great house”), not a personal name.

chapters.n: This king of Egypt descended from Ham, Noah’s son, and through his mother from the Canaanites. Abraham is explaining Egypt’s royal lineage.
From this lineage came the Egyptian people, preserving the Canaanite line in that land.

f.g: Here, descendants of an ancient people of that name; see Moses 7:6-8.

chapters.n: Egypt was first discovered by Ham’s daughter, Egyptus, whose name Abraham says means “that which is forbidden” in Chaldean.

f.g: A Greek/Latin-style form of Egypt’s name (Greek Aigyptos).

chapters.n: When she found the land it was flooded; she later settled her sons there. Abraham says the “curse” — a restriction on priesthood — continued through this line.

f.g: Perhaps after the Flood, or reflecting the Nile’s yearly flooding of Egypt.

chapters.n: Egypt’s first government was set up by Pharaoh, eldest son of Egyptus, following Ham’s patriarchal (father-led) pattern.

f.g: government led by the father or head of the family line.

chapters.n: This first Pharaoh was righteous and wise, trying to copy the order of Adam and Noah. Noah blessed him with earthly blessings and wisdom but not with priesthood rights.

f.w: cursed him as pertaining to the Priesthood
f.g: denied him the patriarchal priesthood right. The Church now teaches that all worthy men may receive the priesthood (Official Declaration 2, 1978).

chapters.n: Because Pharaoh’s line lacked the priesthood right, later Pharaohs tried to claim it falsely from Noah through Ham. Abraham’s father was drawn into their idolatry.

f.g: gladly, eagerly — they wanted to claim it.

f.w: my father was led away by their idolatry

chapters.n: Abraham promises to trace a chronology from himself back to Creation, since he possesses the ancient records.

f.g: to describe or trace out in detail.

chapters.n: After the priest’s death, the famine God had foretold for Chaldea comes to pass.
The famine spreads through Chaldea and torments Abraham’s father, Terah, who then repents of trying to kill his son. Hard times soften his heart — at least for a time.

f.g: Terah (Genesis 11:26-32; Abraham 2:5).

chapters.n: The Lord preserved the patriarchs’ records in Abraham’s hands, including knowledge of the creation, planets, and stars. Abraham will write some of this for his descendants — setting up chapters 3–5.

f.w: the planets, and of the stars
for the benefit of my posterity

chapters.n: The famine God foretold grows severe; Abraham’s brother Haran dies, while their father Terah remains alive in Ur. Hardship sets the stage for the family’s departure.

f.g: grow severe.

chapters.n: Abraham marries Sarai, and his brother Nahor marries Milcah, the daughter of their late brother Haran — keeping the family close-knit.

f.g: Later renamed Sarah, “princess” (Genesis 17:15).

chapters.n: Abraham recalls the Lord’s earlier command: leave your country, your relatives, and your father’s house for a land God will show you. Faith often begins with leaving the familiar behind.

f.w: get thee out of thy country

chapters.n: Abraham leaves Ur for Canaan, taking his nephew Lot, Lot’s wife, and Sarai. His father Terah follows, and they stop at a place they name Haran — perhaps after Abraham’s deceased brother.

f.g: named.

chapters.n: The famine ends, and Terah decides to stay in Haran because of its rich pastures — and because he returns to idolatry. Abraham’s father does not complete the journey of faith.

f.g: lessened, came to an end.
stayed.

chapters.n: Abraham and Lot pray, and the Lord appears, telling Abraham to take Lot and leave Haran. Abraham will be God’s minister in a land his descendants will inherit forever — on condition that they obey.

f.w: when they hearken to my voice

chapters.n: The Lord describes His power: heaven is His home, earth His footstool, the sea obeys Him, and wind and fire serve as His chariot. The God who calls Abraham can keep His promises.

f.w: the wind and the fire to be my chariot

chapters.n: The Lord again reveals His name, Jehovah, and declares that He knows the end from the beginning. Because He sees all, Abraham can trust His protection.

f.w: I know the end from the beginning

chapters.n: The heart of the Abrahamic covenant: Abraham will become a great nation, be richly blessed, and his descendants will carry the gospel ministry and priesthood to every nation.

f.w: bear this ministry and Priesthood unto all nations

chapters.n: Everyone who receives the gospel will be counted as Abraham’s seed and bless him as their father. Covenant identity, not just bloodline, makes someone part of Abraham’s family.

God promises blessings to those who bless Abraham, and that all families of the earth will be blessed through his priesthood and literal descendants — with the blessings of the gospel and eternal life.

f.w: I will bless them that bless thee
all the families of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: After the Lord withdraws, Abraham reflects with joy: he had earnestly sought God, and now he has found Him.
Abraham remembers how God’s angel saved him from the idolatrous priests and resolves to obey and depart in peace.
Abraham leaves Haran as commanded, with Lot. Here he is said to be 62 years old; Genesis 12:4 gives 75, a difference that has been discussed but not definitively resolved.

f.g: Genesis 12:4 gives Abraham’s age as 75 when leaving Haran.

chapters.n: Abraham takes Sarai, Lot, their possessions, and the “souls” they had won in Haran — converts or household members who joined them — and they travel as tent-dwellers toward Canaan.

f.g: possessions, property.

f.w: the souls that we had won in Haran
f.g: Likely people converted to the Lord or joined to their household (compare Genesis 12:5, “the souls that they had gotten”).

chapters.n: Living in tents, Abraham found that eternity itself — God — was their shelter, rock, and salvation as they traveled through Jershon toward Canaan.

f.g: A place on the route to Canaan, known only from this record (unrelated to the Book of Mormon land of Jershon).

chapters.n: In Jershon, Abraham builds an altar, offers sacrifice, and prays that the famine would spare his father’s household — showing love for the family that once tried to harm him.
They pass on to Shechem (“Sechem”) in the plains of Moreh, entering Canaanite territory. Surrounded by idolatry, Abraham prays devoutly and offers sacrifice.

f.g: Shechem, near modern Nablus in the central hill country (Genesis 12:6).
Hebrew, possibly “teacher”; Genesis 12:6 mentions “the plain [or oak] of Moreh.”

chapters.n: In answer to his prayers the Lord appears again and promises this land to Abraham’s descendants.

f.w: Unto thy seed will I give this land

chapters.n: Abraham moves to a mountain between Bethel and Hai (Ai), pitches his tent, builds another altar, and calls on the Lord. Wherever he settled, he made a place to worship.

f.g: Hebrew “house of God,” a site north of Jerusalem later important to Jacob (Genesis 28:19).
Ai, a town east of Bethel (Genesis 12:8; Joshua 7:2).

chapters.n: Abraham keeps moving south, but the famine continues and grows severe, so he decides to go down to Egypt temporarily.

f.g: to stay temporarily as a foreigner.

chapters.n: As they approach Egypt, the Lord warns Abraham that Sarai’s beauty will attract attention.

f.g: beautiful.

chapters.n: The Lord explains the danger: Egyptians who learn she is his wife may kill Abraham to take her.

f.g: in this way.

chapters.n: The Lord instructs that Sarai should say she is Abraham’s sister so his life will be spared. Genesis 20:12 notes she was in fact his half-sister; here the instruction comes directly from God.
Abraham shares the Lord’s instructions with Sarai and asks for her help. Their lives depend on trusting God and each other in a dangerous foreign land.

f.g: please.

f.w: my soul shall live because of thee

chapters.n: Abraham explains that God had given him the Urim and Thummim while he lived in Ur — a sacred instrument used to receive revelation. Through it he will see the heavens.

f.g: Hebrew, often rendered “lights and perfections”; a divinely prepared instrument for revelation (Exodus 28:30; D&C 17:1; Joseph Smith—History 1:35).

chapters.n: Abraham sees that the stars are vast, and one of them is nearest to God’s throne, surrounded by other great stars.

f.w: nearest unto the throne of God

chapters.n: The Lord calls these the “governing ones.” The greatest, Kolob, is nearest to God and governs all the heavenly bodies of the same order as our earth. The lesson points beyond astronomy to God’s orderly rule.

f.g: Possibly related to the Semitic root qlb, “heart” or “center,” or to kokab, “star.”

chapters.n: On Kolob one revolution equals one day of the Lord’s time — a thousand of our years. God’s timescale differs vastly from ours.

f.g: complete turns or cycles.

chapters.n: The Lord teaches that the moon (“lesser light”) is “above” the earth in its reckoning because its time moves more slowly — its cycles are fewer than earth’s days.

f.g: the counting or measuring of time.

chapters.n: God tells Abraham he has seen these facts for himself and is being given to know the “set times” of the earth, sun, and moon — the God-ordained order of time.

f.g: the appointed time or cycle fixed by God.

chapters.n: The moon’s cycle is longer in its reckoning than the earth’s daily cycle.

f.w: the set time of the lesser light

chapters.n: Where two such levels exist, there will be another above them — a body whose time runs longer still. Abraham is learning a principle of hierarchy.
This ascending order continues body by body until one reaches Kolob, which keeps the Lord’s time and governs all bodies of our order near God’s throne.

f.g: near.

f.w: Kolob is set nigh unto the throne of God

chapters.n: Abraham is allowed to know the “set time” of all the light-giving stars, up to the throne of God.

f.w: the set time of all the stars

chapters.n: Abraham talks with the Lord face to face, as friends talk, and the Lord tells him about His creations.
With tender words — “My son, my son” — the Lord touches Abraham’s eyes, and he sees God’s creations multiply without end. Compare Moses’s similar vision of worlds without number.

f.w: I could not see the end thereof

chapters.n: God teaches Abraham names for the heavenly bodies: Shinehah (sun), Kokob (star), Olea (moon), and Kokaubeam (stars). Kokob and Kokaubeam closely resemble Hebrew kokab and kokabim.

f.g: Compare Hebrew kokabim, “stars.”

chapters.n: At night, under these stars, the Lord promises to multiply Abraham’s descendants beyond counting, like the stars and the sands.
God shows Abraham these things before he enters Egypt so that he can teach them there. Abraham will share this knowledge of the heavens with the Egyptians.
The principle restated: wherever one thing is above another, something greater still exists. Kolob is greatest among the stars Abraham has seen because it is nearest to God.
If the moon is above the earth, another body may be above it. And whatever God sets His heart to do, He will do.

f.w: there is nothing that the Lord thy God shall take in his heart to do but what he will do it

chapters.n: Now the lesson moves from stars to spirits: even if one spirit is more intelligent than another, both are eternal — without beginning or end. “Gnolaum” means eternal.

f.g: Compare Hebrew ‘olam, “eternity, forever.”

chapters.n: Just as stars rise in greatness, spirits differ in intelligence, and God is more intelligent than them all. This is the key to the whole astronomy lesson.

f.w: I am more intelligent than they all

chapters.n: The Lord reminds Abraham that He sent His angel to rescue him from Elkenah’s priest — the God of all the heavens is personally aware of Abraham.

f.w: sent his angel to deliver thee

chapters.n: God dwells among all His creations and rules with perfect wisdom over every intelligence. He “came down” to teach Abraham — showing that greatness for God means condescending to lift others.

f.g: practical wisdom and good judgment.

f.w: I came down in the beginning in the midst of all the intelligences

chapters.n: Abraham is shown the spirits (“intelligences”) organized before the world, among whom were many “noble and great ones.”

f.g: Here, the spirits of God’s children in their premortal state.

chapters.n: God stands among these good spirits and chooses them as His rulers. He tells Abraham he was one of them, chosen before birth — a teaching known as foreordination.

f.w: thou wast chosen before thou wast born

chapters.n: One “like unto God” — the premortal Jesus Christ — proposes to go down and organize an earth from existing materials as a home for these spirits. Creation is organizing, not making from nothing.

f.w: one among them that was like unto God
we will take of these materials

chapters.n: The earth’s purpose is a test: to “prove” God’s children and see if they will obey all His commands. Mortality is a school of choice.

f.g: test, try.

f.w: to see if they will do all things

chapters.n: Those who keep their “first estate” (premortal life) receive a body and mortal life; those who keep their “second estate” (mortal life) receive glory forever. Each stage of faithfulness leads to more.

f.g: premortal existence; compare Jude 1:6.
mortal life on earth.

chapters.n: God asks, “Whom shall I send?” One like the Son of Man — Christ — answers, “Here am I, send me.” Another (Lucifer) also volunteers, but God chooses the first.

f.w: like unto the Son of Man
f.g: Jesus Christ in His premortal state.

chapters.n: The rejected one becomes angry, rebels, and loses his first estate, and many follow him. This is the War in Heaven; Satan and his followers never receive mortal bodies.
Abraham’s creation account opens with a council: “Let us go down.” The Gods — plural — organize and form the heavens and earth, shaping existing material rather than creating from nothing.
Once formed, the earth is empty and dark, covered by deep water, while the Spirit of the Gods broods over it like a bird warming its nest — life is about to come.

f.g: Compare Genesis 1:2, “without form, and void” (Hebrew tohu wa-bohu).
hovering protectively, as a bird over its eggs; a fitting sense of the Hebrew merahefet.

chapters.n: The Gods command light into existence, and light appears. Light is the first gift of creation.
The Gods “comprehended” the light — they understood it fully — and divided it from the darkness. Compare Genesis, where God “saw” the light was good.

f.g: understood fully; compare John 1:5.

chapters.n: The Gods name light Day and darkness Night, establishing the first cycle of night and day. Abraham speaks of creative “times” rather than strict 24-hour days.
The Gods plan an “expanse” to separate waters above from waters below. Abraham’s “expanse” clarifies the KJV word “firmament.”

f.g: Hebrew raqia‘, a spread-out sky; the KJV translates it “firmament.”

chapters.n: The Gods “ordered” the expanse, and it was done exactly as commanded. A recurring theme in Abraham: creation obeys its Creators.
The expanse is named Heaven (the sky), closing the second creative time.

f.g: Here, the visible sky or atmosphere.

chapters.n: The Gods order the waters to gather in one place so dry land can appear, and it happens as ordered.

f.w: let the earth come up dry

chapters.n: The dry land is named Earth and the gathered waters Great Waters. The Gods see that they were obeyed — Abraham emphasizes obedience where Genesis says “it was good.”

f.w: the Gods saw that they were obeyed
f.g: Genesis 1:10 reads “God saw that it was good.”

chapters.n: The Gods prepare the earth to bring forth grass, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees, each reproducing its own kind.

f.g: according to its own kind or species.

chapters.n: The earth is organized so each plant comes from its own seed and can only reproduce its own kind — a stable, orderly pattern of life.

f.w: whose seed could only bring forth the same in itself

chapters.n: The Gods “numbered the days,” completing the third time. The word “time” suggests creative periods of undetermined length.

f.g: Abraham uses “time” where Genesis has “day,” leaving the duration open.

chapters.n: The Gods organize lights in the sky to separate day and night and to mark signs, seasons, days, and years — giving humanity a calendar and a way to read time.
These lights are to shine upon the earth, and it is done.

f.w: to give light upon the earth

chapters.n: The two great lights — sun and moon — are organized to rule day and night, along with the stars. Chapter 3 gave Abraham a deeper view of these same bodies.
The Gods place these lights in the heavens to illuminate the earth and divide light from darkness.

f.w: to rule over the day and over the night

chapters.n: A verse found only in Abraham: the Gods watched what they had commanded “until they obeyed.” Creation is pictured as patient, purposeful work over time.

f.g: kept watch over; implies patient attention through a process.

chapters.n: Night and day mark the close of the fourth time.
The Gods plan for the waters to teem with living creatures and for birds to fly across the open sky.

f.g: Abraham often speaks of preparing or planning, suggesting this chapter describes the plan before the physical creation of chapter 5.

chapters.n: The waters are prepared for great sea creatures, swimming life, and birds of every kind. The Gods see that their plan is good and will be obeyed.

f.g: Hebrew tanninim — great sea creatures in general.

chapters.n: The Gods plan to bless these creatures to multiply and fill the seas and earth. Fruitfulness is a blessing from God.
Night and day mark the fifth time.
The earth is prepared to bring forth land creatures: cattle, creeping things, and wild beasts, each after its kind.

f.g: small animals that move close to the ground — insects, reptiles, and the like.

chapters.n: The earth is organized to bring forth every kind of land animal, and the Gods foresee that it will obey.

f.w: the Gods saw they would obey

chapters.n: The crowning act: the Gods counsel together and plan to form man in their own image and likeness, giving humanity stewardship over all creatures.

f.w: in our image, after our likeness

f.g: rule as a steward, with responsibility for what is entrusted.

chapters.n: The Gods go down to organize mankind in their own image, male and female. Both men and women bear the divine image.
The Gods bless man and woman: to have children, fill the earth, subdue it, and care for its creatures.

f.g: in 1611 English, “to fill.”
to bring under control and make productive.

chapters.n: Seed-bearing plants and fruit are given to humans as food. “Meat” here simply means food.

f.g: food in general, not just animal flesh.

chapters.n: Animals, birds, and creeping things are also given life and green plants for food. Every creature has its provision in God’s plan.
The Gods resolve to carry out all they have planned and foresee that creation will be “very obedient.” The sixth time ends with the whole plan in place.

f.g: Genesis 1:31 reads “very good.”

chapters.n: The Gods resolve to complete the heavens, the earth, and everything in them. Chapter 4 was largely the plan; now it will be carried out.

f.g: multitudes — all the beings and things that fill the heavens and earth.

f.w: finish the heavens and the earth

chapters.n: The Gods agree to end their counseled work on the seventh time and to rest from it.
The Gods set apart the seventh time as holy, as part of their council’s decisions. The Sabbath is rooted in the pattern of creation itself.

f.g: made holy, set apart for God.

chapters.n: The Gods now come down and actually form the heavens and the earth, bringing about what they had planned.

f.g: here, the origins or history of the heavens and earth.

f.w: the Gods came down and formed

chapters.n: Everything was done exactly as previously counseled — every plant planned before it grew. No rain had yet fallen, and there was no man to till the ground.

f.w: before it was in the earth

f.g: to cultivate, work the soil.

chapters.n: Instead of rain, a mist rose from the earth and watered the ground — preparing it for life.
The Gods form man’s body from the dust and place his preexisting spirit into it, breathing life into him. Abraham uniquely clarifies that the man’s spirit was put into the body.

f.w: took his spirit (that is, the man's spirit), and put it into him

f.g: body and spirit together (D&C 88:15).

chapters.n: The Gods plant a garden eastward in Eden and place the man there. The man is described as a spirit placed in a formed body.

f.g: Hebrew, perhaps “delight” or “pleasure.”

chapters.n: The garden grows beautiful and fruitful trees, including the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil — the two trees at the center of the Fall story.

f.w: the tree of knowledge of good and evil

chapters.n: A river flows out of Eden to water the garden and then divides into four branches.

f.g: four headwaters or branches; Genesis 2:11-14 names them.

chapters.n: Man is placed in Eden to care for and guard it. Work and stewardship were part of God’s plan from the start.

f.g: to tend, cultivate.

f.w: to dress it and to keep it

chapters.n: The Gods give man freedom to eat of every tree in the garden — a generous permission before the one restriction.

Only the tree of knowledge is forbidden, with the warning of death. Abraham adds that the “day” of death followed the Lord’s time — Kolob’s reckoning of a thousand years — since Adam had not yet been given earthly time.
The Gods declare it is not good for man to be alone and plan to make a “help meet” — a fitting partner for him.

f.g: a helper suited to him; Hebrew ‘ezer kenegdo, “a help corresponding to him.” ‘Ezer is also used of God (Psalms 33:20).

chapters.n: Adam is put into a deep sleep, and a rib is taken from his side. The image suggests a partner who stands beside him.

f.g: in its place.

chapters.n: From the rib the Gods form a woman and bring her to the man. God Himself introduces the first marriage.
Adam recognizes her as part of himself — “bone of my bones” — and calls her Woman because she came from man.

f.g: Hebrew ’ishah, sounding like ’ish, “man.”

chapters.n: This is the foundation of marriage: a man leaves his parents and holds fast to his wife, and they become one. Jesus later quoted this verse.

f.g: cling to, stay joined to.

chapters.n: Adam and Eve are naked and unashamed — a picture of innocence before the Fall.
The Gods form the animals and bring them to Adam to name. Naming them shows Adam’s God-given stewardship and understanding.

f.w: to see what he would call them

chapters.n: Adam names all the animals, and for him a fitting partner was found — Eve, who would join him in God’s plan.
